From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwoodinference.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwoodinference.com>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Aug 2026 14:22:10 -0700
Subject: RE: Dedicated sizing kickoff — analysis + assumptions)

Neha / Ben — I ran a conservative projection from the supplied CSV. Notes and assumptions up front: 
- Model: customer plans to serve a 16B-parameter open model quantized to 4-bit (throughput profile similar to our "midslab" baseline). We used per-token service time = 0.6ms on an H100-instance equivalent for single-request, single-stream runs (no KV cache).
- Caching: assume prefix/KV caching will reduce average decoding tokens by ~28% for their multi-turn flows (they indicated repeated system prompts).
- Batching: continuous batching can increase throughput but adds batching latency; we assume 10–15ms batching window for background/bulk and sub-ms for interactive small requests.

Traffic numbers from Aisha: median 230 tokens, p95 1,100 tokens, peak conc users 420. Convert to steady tokens/sec baseline: 
- Baseline concurrency conversion: assume 420 conc users * 3 calls/session * median 230 tokens * 0.0006s/token => CPU/GPU time demand per second ~ 173.7s of GPU compute per second (i.e., 173.7 GPU-seconds per wall second).
- After KV caching (28% reduction) effective compute demand -> 125.1 GPU-seconds per wall second.

Mapping to GPUs (H100 80GB perf baseline):
- One H100-equivalent can sustain ~8.5 GPU-seconds of decode per wall second for this model profile (sustained with efficient kernels and moderate batching).
- Required GPUs (sustained) = 125.1 / 8.5 ≈ 15 GPUs => recommend 16 GPUs for base committed slab to cover baseline with a small rounding buffer.

Headroom & surge planning: 
- Marketing bursts (2–3x baseline) mean peak demand could be 32–48 GPUs equivalent for short windows. We recommend: 
  * Base reserved pool: 16 GPUs (Committed Dedicated) — covers normal peak with caching.
  * Burst pool (on-demand reserved or shared capacity): additional 24 GPUs available for up to 8 hours/day (auto-burst policy).
  * Safety buffer: 20% additional capacity for unexpected tail (round up to 48 total GPUs if burst fully used).

Latency SLOs: 
- For interactive p95 < 450ms: With the above mapping and KV caching turned on, predicted p95 ~ 380–420ms (includes network + decode + small batching).
- p99 tail: may hit 800–1,000ms during full-burst if not throttled; recommend two mitigations: 
  1) Stronger prefix caching for high-frequency prompts to lower p99.
  2) Fallback policy to smaller, faster model variant (e.g., 7B quantized variant) when token queue exceeds a threshold to preserve interactive latency.

Operational recommendations: 
- Autoscaling policy: aggressive vertical burst (add whole GPUs) with pre-warmed images and short cold start mitigation (warm pool).
- Observability: route p99, queue depth, KV cache hit ratio to console dashboards and add regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
- Billing: project committed monthly tokens and burst bill separately; recommend a 12-month commit for lower unit price on the 16-GPU base.

Attachments: I exported the per-minute token-supply workbook with the GPU mapping (caledonia_token_model.xlsx).

--

Quick add from a pricing/CS perspective: 
- Recommend we model two purchase options in the MOP: (A) 12-month commit for 16 GPUs + burst pool metered; (B) 6-month commit for 12 GPUs + larger metered burst. The unit economics change ~12–18% between these.
- SLA ask: if they require a >99.95% uptime SLA for the committed pool, we need an explicit uplift (we'll include it in the draft commercial term sheet).
- Risk note: headroom cushion must be explicit in the SOW (we include the 20% safety buffer language).

I attached a starter M&A plan/ToR doc — I can convert to a polished MAP for procurement.
